But we shall easily be disentangled from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted, that he wished at that time to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness by earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death by bodily punishments, for that time when he was delivering his Testament, still in some way wrapped up, to the Israelite people.

4 Another difference between the Old and New Testaments is established in the figures, in that the former, with the truth absent, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body, whereas the latter exhibits the present truth and a solid body. And mention of this is made almost everywhere the New Testament is opposed to the Old, yet its treatment is more extensive in the Epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There, the Apostle disputes against those who thought that the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the entire religion. To refute this error, he assumes <margin>Psalm 110:4</margin> what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is bestowed upon him, it is certain that the priesthood in which others were substituted as successors to others every day was to be abolished. Furthermore, he proves the pre-eminence of the institution of this new priest by the fact that it is established by an oath <margin>Hebrews 7:11, 19; 9:9; 10:1</margin>. He adds afterward that in that translation of the priesthood, there is also a change of the Testament. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, since the weakness of the Law was such that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to explain what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not make its worshippers perfect according to conscience, and that through the victims of beasts, it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow in the very thing of future goods, not a living image of the things, and that therefore it had no other duty than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here we must see in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, and the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, there would be a great disagreement between the two Testaments, but since the status of the question leads us elsewhere, we must tend toward finding the truth. Let us, therefore, place in the middle the covenant which God ratified once and for all as eternal and never to perish. The completion of that covenant, from which it finally derives its status as ratified and firm, is Christ. While such confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are like solemn symbols of confirmation. This came into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. Although these were merely accidents of the covenant, or certainly accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories, yet because they were instruments of administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as it is accustomed to be given to other Sacraments. Therefore, in sum, the Old Testament is called in this place the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprised in ceremonies and sacrifices. Since nothing solid underlies it unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification was acquired once for all for the elect, and transgressions were obliterated, which remained under the Law. But if you prefer it so, take it thus: the Old Testament was the Lord's, which was delivered wrapped up in the shadowy and ineffective observance of ceremonies, and therefore it was temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense until it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. But then it was finally made new and eternal, after it was consecrated and stabilized by the blood of Christ. Whence the cup which Christ holds out to his disciples in the Supper, he calls the cup of the New Testament <margin>Matthew 26:28</margin> in his blood, to signify that the Testament of God then truly attains its own truth, through which it becomes new and eternal, while it is sealed by his blood.

5 From this, it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led by the pedagogy <note>original: "pædagogia"; referring to the Law as a tutor or guide</note> of the Law to Christ <margin>Galatians 3:24; 4:1</margin> before he himself was exhibited in the flesh. He acknowledges that they were also children and heirs of God, but who, because of childhood, had to be kept under the custody of a tutor. For it was fitting that, the sun of justice not yet having risen, there should be neither such splendor of revelation nor such perspicacity of understanding. Thus, therefore, the Lord dispensed the light of his Word to them, so that they might see it from afar and still obscurely. Therefore, Paul marks this thinness of intelligence with the word childhood, which the Lord willed to be exercised by the elements of this world and external little observances, as if they were rules of childish discipline, until Christ should shine forth, through whom it was necessary that the cognition of the faithful people should mature. Christ himself marked this distinction when he said that the Law and the Prophets were until John, and from that time the kingdom of God is evangelized <margin>Matthew 11:13</margin>. What did the Law and the Prophets profit the men of their time? Namely, they provided a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested clearly, and they prefigured it shining from afar. But where Christ can be pointed out with the finger, the kingdom of God is laid open. For in him are deposited all the treasures of wisdom and intelligence <margin>Colossians 2:9</margin>, by which one penetrates near to the very sanctuaries of heaven.

<summary>Calvin explains that the Old Testament ceremonies were temporary, shadowy figures intended to lead the people toward the eventual perfection found in Christ, who established the New Testament through his blood.</summary>
<keywords>Old Testament, New Testament, Law and Gospel, Priesthood of Christ, Covenant, Ceremonies, Pedagogy of the Law</keywords>
